steps.action:
# The Last Light

The storm had been building for three days before it finally arrived.

Maren could feel it in her knees first, the way the pressure dropped and her joints filled with a dull, grinding ache that she had learned to trust more than any barometer. She climbed the hundred and twelve steps of Cormorant Point Light the way she did every evening, one hand trailing the curved stone wall, her lantern swinging from the other. The steps were worn smooth in the center, dished out by a century of keepers before her, and she often thought about that — about the accumulated weight of all those careful feet, all those people who had made this same climb in the dark, in the rain, in the fog, in the obliterating silence of January.

She was the last of them. She knew that. The Coast Guard had told her as much last spring, when the regional supervisor had driven out in his white truck with the blue stripe and sat at her kitchen table drinking her coffee and explaining, with genuine discomfort, what automated systems could now do. She had listened politely. She had refilled his cup. And when he left, she had climbed her hundred and twelve steps and lit the light herself, the same way her father had taught her thirty-one years ago, when her hands were small and the brass fittings were larger than her fists.

Tonight the light came on without ceremony, as it always did. The great Fresnel lens — fourth order, a beauty, one of the few still operational on this stretch of coast — caught the flame and scattered it outward in its slow, patient revolution. One flash every four seconds. That was Cormorant Point's signature, its particular word in the long conversation between shore and sea. Every lighthouse spoke its own language of intervals, and mariners learned to read them the way others read faces.

Maren sat in the watch room below the lantern room and looked out at the Atlantic going dark.

The waves were running long and heavy from the northeast, the kind that didn't break so much as heave, rising and falling like a breathing chest. The horizon had disappeared an hour ago into a low ceiling of cloud the color of a bruise. She could already hear the wind beginning to articulate itself around the tower's corners, finding the seams, testing the old mortar.

She opened her logbook. November 14th. Wind NNE 22 knots, increasing. Barometric pressure 29.1 and falling. Visibility declining. She wrote in a small, careful hand that her father would have recognized, because he had taught her that too.

Her father, Edmund Vaas, had been keeper here for twenty-six years. His father before him for nineteen. Maren had grown up in the keeper's cottage below, a white clapboard house that was always slightly damp, always smelling of salt and lamp oil and the particular woolly warmth of fishermen's sweaters drying by the stove. She had done her schoolwork at the kitchen table while her father climbed his steps. She had learned the names of clouds before she learned the names of the states. She had known, from earliest childhood, the difference between the sound a calm sea made and the sound it made when it meant business.

This sea, tonight, meant business.

She poured coffee from her thermos — she still brought a thermos, still kept the old routines — and thought about the vessels she'd marked in the traffic logs over the past week. A container ship, the *Alvara Dos Santos*, running the coastal route south. Three lobster boats out of Whitmore Harbor, though they'd have run for port by now, any captain worth his license would have. A small sailing vessel, forty feet or so, that she'd tracked through her binoculars two days ago. The sight of it had nagged at her since. It had been sailing north, which struck her as contrary, and moving with a kind of deliberate stubbornness she recognized as the behavior of someone who either knew something she didn't or didn't know something she did.

She reached for her binoculars now, more out of habit than hope. Visibility was down to perhaps a mile. The water was the color of pewter beaten by a hammer. She swept the glass along the horizon and found nothing but chaos.

Then she found something.

It was hard to be sure. The wave tops were blowing off in long white streamers and the whole sea surface had a pale, confused brightness that could trick the eye into seeing shapes. But she held the binoculars steady and waited, the way her father had taught her. *Don't chase what you see*, he'd said. *Wait for it to come to you.*

It came to her. A hull, rising on a swell. Dark, low in the water. No running lights.

She was already reaching for the radio.

---

The sailing vessel was called *Henriette*. She was a 1962 wooden ketch, forty-three feet, out of Gloucester, and she had blown her headsail and lost steerage an hour ago in the leading edge of the storm. Her crew was two: a man named Gerald Poole, who was sixty-eight and had been sailing for forty years and was therefore not panicked but was deeply, professionally worried, and his daughter Sophie, who was twenty-nine, seven months pregnant, and had come on this passage against her husband's better judgment, which she was presently, silently, acknowledging.

Gerald had been trying to raise anyone on VHF Channel 16 for twenty minutes when a woman's voice came back to him, calm and clear, cutting through the static.

"*Henriette*, this is Cormorant Point Light. I have you on visual. What is your situation, over."

He told her. His voice was steady, but his hands on the radio were not.

Maren took down everything he said: position, crew, the nature of the damage. She was already calculating as she wrote. The *Henriette* was northeast of the point, being pushed southwest by the wind, which was, she noted with the particular detached gratitude of someone accustomed to looking for mercy in difficult circumstances, almost exactly the right direction. If the vessel held together and Gerald could maintain even minimal steerage with the main alone, the wind itself was going to push them toward the coast, toward Cutter's Cove, which was not a good harbor in any real sense of the word but was a harbor of last resort — a notch in the rocks with a gravel bar where a boat could be run aground and held.

She told him all this. She told him in the clear, measured way she described everything, as if the information were simply facts to be transferred, as if there were nothing at stake.

"There's a light on the point," she said. "One flash every four seconds. You keep that on your port quarter and you're running the right direction. Don't let it come around to your starboard. When you see the coast rocks, you're going to see a break in them — it's not much, maybe forty feet across, and there's a green flasher on the north side of it. You go through the middle of that gap. The bottom inside is gravel. Don't be afraid to drive her up on it. Better the boat than you."

There was a pause. Then Gerald's voice, careful: "There's a pregnant woman aboard."

"I know," Maren said. "I heard you. Go through the middle of the gap."

She got on the phone to the Coast Guard station at Whitmore and reported the situation and gave them the position and told them what she'd told Gerald. The duty officer asked if she thought the vessel was in immediate danger of sinking. She said she thought the vessel was in danger of being in danger, which was enough. He said he'd dispatch the forty-seven footer. She said fine, but to tell them that if the *Henriette* got her bearings right, she'd be on the gravel at Cutter's Cove before they arrived, so to come in around the headland from the south because the north approach would be impassable in this.

The duty officer, who was twenty-four years old and had been at the station for eight months, took this guidance without question. Something in her voice made you do that.

Maren pulled on her oilskin. Then she climbed back up the hundred and twelve steps, opened the hatch to the lantern room, and stood in the full roar of the storm with her hand over her eyes.

She could still see the dark shape of the *Henriette*, barely, rising and disappearing and rising again. The great lens behind her threw its arm of light out over the water every four seconds with absolute patience, the way it had done for a hundred and fourteen years.

*One flash every four seconds. Keep it on your port quarter.*

She watched.

---

It took forty minutes.

Gerald Poole brought the *Henriette* through the gap on a wave that was bigger than anything he'd handled in forty years of sailing, a dark green mountain of water that stood up in the gap and then flattened into a hissing rush of foam, and the boat surfed on the face of it and hit the gravel bar with a grinding crash that knocked Sophie off her feet and split three planks on the starboard bow.

Then the wave receded and the boat was there. Solid. Canted at fifteen degrees, bow buried in gravel, but there.

Gerald sat in the cockpit for thirty seconds and did not move.

Sophie climbed out of the companionway and stood in the knee-deep surge and looked at her hands for a moment as if checking that they were still attached.

"Dad," she said.

"Yeah."

"We're on the ground."

"Yeah," Gerald said again. He sounded like a man who had just set down something extraordinarily heavy.

The Coast Guard boat arrived twenty minutes later, and the crew helped Sophie and Gerald ashore with efficient, cheerful professionalism and wrapped them in blankets and asked the questions they were required to ask. Gerald answered all of them. Sophie stood apart from the activity, looking back across the water at the lighthouse.

"Who was that?" she asked the young Guardsman next to her. "The woman on the radio."

He glanced toward the light. "Maren Vaas," he said. "She's the keeper out at Cormorant Point. She's been there since—" He tried to remember. "I don't know. Forever, basically."

Sophie looked at the light. One flash. Dark. One flash. Dark.

"Are there others?" she asked. "Other keepers like her?"

The young man's expression shifted in a way that was not quite a smile and not quite something sadder. "No," he said. "She's the last one."

Sophie watched the light a moment longer.

"Someone should tell her," she said, "that she did a good thing tonight."

"They probably should," the young Guardsman agreed. "Though I don't think she'd make much of it."

---

Maren logged the incident at 11:47 p.m. *Vessel* Henriette *brought safely to Cutter's Cove gravel bar under own power. Crew of two, condition reported good. Coast Guard 47-footer on scene 00:04.* She noted the barometric pressure, which had dropped another point. She noted the wind speed, which had increased to forty-one knots. She noted the wave height, which she estimated at twelve to fifteen feet in open water, eight at the point.

Then she closed the logbook and sat for a while in the watch room and drank the last of her cold coffee and listened to the storm work itself over the tower, searching for a way in.

The light went around and around and around.

She thought about the automated system the supervisor had described — the cameras and the sensors and the algorithm that would, in theory, do what she did. It would monitor. It would transmit. It would receive. It would, in the language of the documentation she'd been sent, *perform continuous environmental assessment and broadcast accurate navigational signals without interruption.*

She did not think the algorithm would know what a pregnant woman on a damaged boat needed to hear.

She did not think the algorithm would say, *don't be afraid to drive her up on it.*

Perhaps she was wrong. Perhaps in time it would learn. She held no grievance against algorithms; she held no grievance against time. These were not things worth grieving over. The light would keep going either way, and the light was what mattered. The light had always been what mattered.

Still.

She climbed the last twelve steps to the lantern room and stood for a moment inside the turning lens, inside the warm, repeated heartbeat of the light, and looked out at the sea through the thick glass as the storm threw itself against everything and the beam went out and out and out, patient as breath, faithful as stone.

Thirty-one years.

A hundred and twelve steps.

One flash every four seconds.

She put her hand flat against the glass and felt the cold of the sea radiating through it.

"All right," she said quietly to no one, to everyone, to the old mariner's sky and the indifferent water and the long line of keepers before her whose dished footsteps she had worn a little smoother every night for three decades.

She said it the way her father had said it when the work was done and the light was burning and there was nothing left to do but trust it.

"All right."

The beam went out again across the dark.
